          Jérémy Jacquet Showing That Not Every Player Needs a Bedding-in Period
        
      
                          
                      Oct 10, 2026
          
                      David Segar / Author, Emily Millen / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
It has been an up-and-down start to the season for Liverpool, but one huge positive has been the early form of new arrival Jérémy Jacquet. So, just how good has the French defender been?
When you get praise from Zinedine Zidane, you know you’ve made it.
Jérémy Jacquet earned his first call-up to the France national team in this latest international break, starting UEFA Nations League games against Türkiye and Italy, and impressing in both.

When asked about the impact of the 21-year-old centre-back in the draw with Italy, Zidane said: “Very good. Very, very good. Brave. He wasn’t afraid to come out a long way. Very good in the duels. He was, once again, very good. I said it four times.”
Unfortunately, Jacquet had to be left out of the return game against Italy on Monday due to what Zidane described as a “slight knock”, but he had already made a solid impression.
That call-up was merited, too. Jacquet has made an excellent start to the season with new club Liverpool, taking to the Premier League like a canard to eau.
When Liverpool signed Jacquet in January, the assumption was he would be eased in slowly.

He was lined up to join the Reds this summer in a reported £60 million deal from Rennes, but with compatriot Ibrahima Konaté leaving for Real Madrid, a gap opened up that Jacquet has gleefully stepped into.
Despite being just 21 years old and playing in France’s second tier just two seasons ago, Jacquet has slipped seamlessly into Premier League football at Anfield.
Liverpool also brought Ronald Araujo in on loan from Barcelona, but he has been deployed at right-back more often than centre-back, with Jacquet trusted by Andoni Iraola to partner Virgil van Dijk.

Jacquet suffered a shoulder injury in his first game for Rennes after confirming his summer switch to Merseyside, then also had a setback ahead of pre-season. But Iraola still backed him from the beginning, even though he was signed before the Spaniard’s own arrival. Jacquet started Liverpool’s opening game of the campaign, and though he came off early in the 2-2 draw at Newcastle United as well as in the stalemate with Nottingham Forest, it was clear he was just having his minutes managed as he got up to full fitness.
Jacquet has started all five of Liverpool’s Premier League games this season, as well as the UEFA Champions League win over Atlético Madrid.

The 1-0 win at Bournemouth last time out made it three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League for Liverpool for the first time since September 2024, and Jacquet played a significant role in that achievement.
So, just what has made Jacquet’s first couple of months in England so impressive?

Back in January, we analysed his game to see why Liverpool were willing to fork out so much money for an inexperienced young defender. Jacquet had shown in his time in France that he was aerially dominant, composed on the ball, and a front-foot defender who could win the ball often.
He has been all that and more already for Liverpool, too.

Jacquet won 75.5% of his aerial duels in Ligue 1 last season, the most of any player to contest at least 40. He has carried that on in England, winning 10 of 13 aerials in the Premier League (76.9%), more than both Van Dijk (71.4%) and Araújo (72.0%). Only Manchester United’s Harry Maguire (17 of 22 – 77.3%) has won a greater proportion among players to have contested 13+ aerials.

He has also been outstanding in ground duels, winning 19 of 25 (76.0%). Of Premier League defenders to have contested 15+ ground duels this season, only Everton’s James Tarkowski has won a greater share (19 of 21 – 90.5%).

A metric called ‘true tackles’ can give an even better idea of his ability. It’s the sum of successful tackles (where possession is regained or when the ball goes out of play and is safe), challenges lost (where a player attempts a tackle and doesn’t connect with the ball) and fouls when attempting a tackle. Jacquet has attempted 15 true tackles in the Premier League this season, with a success rate of 73.3%; no player to have attempted as many has a higher win percentage.

His ability in possession has also made him suited to Iraola’s style of play. At Bournemouth, the Spaniard loved his centre-backs getting the ball forward with their progressive passing, and that has continued at Liverpool. Jacquet has played 57 passes into the opposition’s final third in the Premier League this season; only Van Dijk (76) and Tottenham’s Jan Paul van Hecke (62) have attempted more.
